questions.q: What is the default marker style for an unordered list (`<ul>`) in HTML5, and which CSS property would you use to change it to squares?
questions.a: The default marker is a solid disc (bullet). To change it to squares, use the CSS property `list-style-type: square;`. A wrong answer (e.g., "circle" or "decimal") reveals the student is confusing default unordered list markers with ordered list numbering or CSS keyword values.

questions.q: Explain the semantic difference between `<ol>` and `<ul>`. Give a real-world example where using `<ol>` would be incorrect even if the items appear in a sequence.
questions.a: `<ol>` implies a meaningful order where changing the sequence changes the meaning (e.g., steps in a recipe). `<ul>` implies a collection where order is arbitrary (e.g., ingredients). Using `<ol>` for a list of team members (where alphabetical order is just presentation, not semantic) would be incorrect. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks any visible sequence justifies `<ol>`, missing the semantic distinction.

questions.q: Write the HTML code for an ordered list that starts at 3, uses lowercase Roman numerals, and contains three items: "Apple", "Banana", "Cherry". Show the rendered output.
questions.a:
```html
  1. Apple
  2. Banana
  3. Cherry
``` Rendered: iii. Apple iv. Banana v. Cherry A wrong answer (e.g., missing `start`, using `type="I"`, or wrong numeral sequence) reveals misunderstanding of attribute interaction or Roman numeral case sensitivity.

questions.q: Compare the structure of a definition list (`<dl>`) with a two-column table (`<table>`). When would you choose `<dl>` over `<table>` for presenting key-value pairs?
questions.a: `<dl>` uses `<dt>` (term) and `<dd>` (description) which are semantically linked; `<table>` uses `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>` for tabular data with rows/columns. Choose `<dl>` for glossaries, metadata, or FAQs where each term has a single description and no column headers are needed. A wrong answer (e.g., "always use tables for alignment") shows lack of semantic HTML awareness and accessibility understanding.

questions.q:
A student writes `
  1. Item 1
    • Subitem A
` but forgets to close the outer `
  • ` before starting the nested `
      `. Is this valid HTML5? What will the browser do?
questions.a: Invalid. In HTML5, a nested list must be inside a parent `<li>`. The browser's parser will implicitly close the parent `<li>` before the `<ul>`, making the sublist a sibling, not a child. The rendered structure becomes two separate list items at the same level. This error reveals the student doesn't understand the content model: `<ul>`/`<ol>` can only be direct children of `<li>`, not of another `<ul>`/`<ol>`.

questions.q: Design a single HTML snippet that uses all three list types (`<ul>`, `<ol>`, `<dl>`) in a nested structure to represent: a course curriculum with modules (ordered), each module's topics (unordered), and a glossary of terms (definition). The snippet must be valid and semantically correct.
questions.a:
```html
  1. Module 1: HTML Basics
    • Tags and Elements
    • Attributes
  2. Module 2: CSS Basics
    • Selectors
    • Box Model
HTML
HyperText Markup Language
CSS
Cascading Style Sheets
``` A poor answer (e.g., mixing list types incorrectly, missing closing tags, or putting `
` inside `
  • ` without reason) shows inability to compose semantic structures for hierarchical content.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: HTML lists are semantic container elements that group related items in a specific order (ordered list <ol>), without implied sequence (unordered list <ul>), or as term-______ pairs (definition list <dl>).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ a webpage for a school magazine.
What is HTML lists? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: HTML lists are semantic container elements that group related items in a specific order (ordered list <ol>), without implied sequence (unordered list <ul>), or as term-description pairs (definition list <dl>).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about HTML lists?
questions.a: Students often think the type attribute on <ol> changes only the visual style (like CSS) and that start works with any type.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to write valid HTML5 code for all three list types, correctly nest lists up to two levels, apply the type, start, and reversed attributes on ordered lists, and explain when to choose each list type based on content semantics.
